newsitem.title: CANADA: INSTANT VIEW - Canada March consumer prices.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Canada March consumer prices.

text.p: Following are reactions to March consumer price data released by Statistics Canada on Tuesday. Canada's unadjusted March consumer price index rose 0.2 percent in the month and 2.0 percent in the year to 137.6. Unadjusted CPI ex-food and energy rose 1.7 percent.

A Reuters survey of economists had forecast the seasonally adjusted CPI to rise 0.1 percent on the month and the undadjusted CPI to rise 0.2 percent on the month. The survey also forecast a 2.0 percent year-over-year rise in the all- items and 1.5 percent rise in the core CPI.

Mark Mullins, chief economist, Midland Walwyn Capital Inc -- "A little higher than expectations in the overall rate. The cause for concern I think is less CPI -- which still even at 0.2 (percent) is very well-behaved -- than the PPI (producer price index) or at least the Canadian equivalent.

"In February, we saw a bit of currency depreciation which flowed through into the raw materials and the industrial prices, ex-energy. And we know already that March saw an even greater decline in the buck and we are still under pressure in April. So I think you are going to see well above expectations increases in producer prices.

Mullins -- "The bottom line is, are we seeing any inflation out there? On consumer prices, the answer is no, things are very steady. We're at the midpoint of the Bank's range or just below it. But on producer prices, we're seeing a little sneaking in.

"We've got a very strong economy right now and a lot of commentators more or less urging the bank to move at least from easy to neutral monetary policy and what that probably means is 75 basis points increase in rates sometime this summer."

Michael Gregory, economist, Lehman Brothers -- "Pretty boring except that core inflation was a little bit faster than expected. Could this be the impact of a depreciating Canadian dollar feeding through the system and very robust domestic demand? We will see heading forward.

"We have seen the Canadian dollar over the past several weeks depreciate from C$1.36-ish to C$1.39-40-ish. That's about three percent. The old rule of thumb is that's worth about a full percentage point on CPI inflation year-over-year.
"There is a little bit of measured price increases coming down the pipe, not necessarily inflation.

Gregory -- "But let's face it, yesterday's wholesale trade number and I suspect today's 0830 (EDT/1230 GMT) retail trade number are showing that demand conditions in Canada are firm and firming. At the same time you have got this spike potentially in CPI inflation due to a depreciating Canadian dollar and I think we will probably see core inflation gravitate towards that two percent level for the time being.
"Every day we go forward, we're getting stronger economic data, a little bit of a surprise on the inflation side, and before you know it, we could have a Bank of Canada rate hike."

Paul Ferley, assistant chief economist, Bank of Montreal -- "We saw some moderation in energy prices which helped move the overall index down to 2.0 percent from 2.2. We were a little bit surprised by the move up in core prices to 1.7 percent, though the pressure seemed narrowly based and the measure still remains in the bottom half of the Bank of Canada's target range so still indicative of minimal price pressure in the system.
"I think it's still indicating a slowing in the overall measure and core prices are still fairly moderate, so I think it argues for the bank to still hold policy steady for now."
